records.title: PoC pilot: base 8k vs symmetric 64k vs Fraise at 100M dense, 500M FineWeb-Edu base tokens
records.summary: Compares the three proof-of-concept models (the 8k/8k transformer, the 64k/64k transformer on the macro tokenizer, and Fraise, 64k in and 8k out) with the same 99.2M-parameter transformer on the same 500M base tokens of FineWeb-Edu text, by held-out bits per byte (BPB), to see what reading a large macro vocabulary costs or gains at equal text. The three imported runs put the 8k/8k transformer first (1.130), the 64k/64k model second (1.194) and Fraise third (1.233). One seed each, more optimizer steps for the macro models, and two training faults later found in both transformer baselines mean this ranking overstates the cost of a 64k vocabulary; the pilot has not been re-run with the fixes.

variants.title: Base 8k/8k transformer (byte-level BPE base-8192)
variants.description: The baseline: a standard transformer reading and writing the 8,192-token byte-level BPE, batch 64 × 512 positions, AdamW 1e-3. It is the small-vocabulary conventional model Fraise has to beat on quality per unit of compute.

variants.title: Symmetric 64k/64k transformer on the macro tokenizer
variants.description: The same transformer reading and writing the 65,536-token macro tokenizer (about 41% fewer positions per byte), batch 32, AdamW 3e-3. It is the large-vocabulary conventional model: Fraise shares its input side and tokenizer, so the two differ only in how the next macro is predicted.

variants.title: Fraise 64k-in / 8k-out (compositional embeddings, 32-d residuals, local decoder)
variants.description: Fraise: macro inputs composed from base-token embeddings plus a 32-dimensional learned residual, the same transformer over macro positions, and a 10.1M-parameter local decoder that predicts the next macro's base tokens and END. Batch 32, AdamW 3e-3, as for the 64k/64k model.

records.protocol: Commit d0fc54e (run from the t3 worktree t3-0e6f556d; dirty). Models: configs/100m/{base,symmetric,fraise}.json (d=768, 14 layers, 12x64 heads, SwiGLU 2048, context 512). Data: FineWeb-Edu sample-10BT in stream order, 500,000,000 base tokens per run, 1 epoch, shuffle_data true. Base: batch 64 (minibatch 32), AdamW 1e-3 (configs/pilot-base.json). Symmetric and Fraise: batch 32, AdamW 3e-3 (configs/pilot-macro.json). Muon 0.02, warmup 200, weight decay 0.01, clip 1.0, BF16 + torch.compile, seed 1337, one seed per variant. Validation every 2,000 steps on CPU over 262,144 base tokens of the 0.05 GB held-out FineWeb-Edu prefix. Compare on validation/bits_per_byte only: validation/loss is per macro for 64k models and per base token for base 8k, so it is not comparable across variants. Note the step-count confound (15,259 vs 17,896 optimizer steps). Runs so far are imported, not re-run under AblationKit.
records.body:
## Why this comparison

The project's claim is that Fraise gives a better tradeoff between language-model quality, global transformer computation, sequence and KV-cache length, and access to the text inside tokens than either conventional baseline. The pilot is the first comparison at a size where the models learn real language: the same 99.2M-parameter transformer (d = 768, 14 layers, context 512 positions) in all three, trained on identical text, with budgets counted in base tokens so that each model sees the same bytes whatever its tokenizer.

Bits per byte (BPB) is the summed negative log-likelihood of the held-out targets, in bits, divided by the UTF-8 bytes those targets cover:

$$
\mathrm{BPB} = \frac{1}{B \ln 2} \sum_{t} -\ln p(x_t \mid x_{<t})
$$

where $B$ is the number of bytes scored. Unlike a per-token loss it does not depend on the tokenizer, so it compares models with 8k and 64k vocabularies directly. Lower is better.

Validation loss is per macro for the 64k models and per base token for the 8k/8k, so only BPB is compared across variants.

## Variants

| Variant | Input / output vocabulary | Batch (steps) | AdamW | Final BPB |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | ---: |
| base-8k (baseline) | 8k / 8k | 64 × 512 (15,259) | 1e-3 | 1.1302 |
| symmetric-64k | 64k / 64k, macro tokenizer | 32 × 512 (17,896) | 3e-3 | 1.1940 |
| fraise | 64k / 8k | 32 × 512 (17,896) | 3e-3 | 1.2332 |

Fraise adds a 10.1M-parameter dense local decoder to the shared transformer (109.3M dense in total). The learning rates are the best of the 38M sweep; the batch for the macro models was a deliberate choice of the project owner, recorded as a decision.

## Reading the result

- All three runs were imported from their files, not re-run under AblationKit; they come from commit d0fc54e in a separate, dirty worktree.
- One seed per variant: seed variance is unmeasured. The pilot report's bootstrap intervals over a larger held-out set (13.5M tokens) cover sampling of the validation text only.
- The macro models took 17% more optimizer steps at a smaller batch and a higher learning rate; at 38M parameters, doubling the 64k/64k model's steps later made no difference.
- Both transformer baselines kept untied embeddings at N(0,1) and had no final LayerNorm. At 38M parameters, fixing both cut the 64k/64k model's gap to the 8k/8k from 0.152 to 0.085 BPB, and a standard 64k BPE closed it. Fraise already normalises its state before its decoder, so the Fraise-against-baseline differences here are also confounded.
- The comparison is at equal text. At equal transformer compute (equal positions) the pilot report finds the answer not established, because the 8k/8k value would have to be read before its learning rate had annealed.

records.title: AdamW learning-rate sweep at 38M dense, 50M FineWeb-Edu base tokens
records.summary: Sweeps the AdamW learning rate over 3e-3, 1e-3 and 3e-4 for each of the 8k/8k transformer, the 64k/64k transformer on the macro tokenizer and Fraise (64k in, 8k out) at 38M parameters and 50M base tokens of text, with Muon fixed at 0.02, to choose learning rates for the 100M pilot. The 8k/8k model is best at 1e-3 (1.4087 bits per byte, BPB) and both macro models at 3e-3, the largest rate tried (64k/64k 1.5602, Fraise 1.5408), so their optimum may be higher; Fraise beats the 64k/64k model at every rate. One seed per run, imported from files, and the transformer runs carry the two training faults found later by the gap audit.

Configs configs/sweep-{lr}.json; minibatch 64, or 16 after an out-of-memory fallback (sweep2.sh; the minibatch actually used is in each run's params). Validation once at the end over 262,144 held-out base tokens. Compare on validation/bits_per_byte only. Runs so far are imported, not re-run under AblationKit.
records.body:
## Why this comparison

The pilot needed a learning rate for each architecture, and the macro models, with larger vocabularies and fewer optimizer steps at equal text, could not be assumed to share the 8k/8k transformer's. Muon updates the transformer's weight matrices and was fixed at 0.02; AdamW updates everything else (embeddings, output heads, Fraise's residuals and gates), so its rate is the one swept.

Bits per byte (BPB) is the summed negative log-likelihood of the held-out targets, in bits, divided by the UTF-8 bytes those targets cover:

$$
\mathrm{BPB} = \frac{1}{B \ln 2} \sum_{t} -\ln p(x_t \mid x_{<t})
$$

where $B$ is the number of bytes scored. Unlike a per-token loss it does not depend on the tokenizer, so it compares models with 8k and 64k vocabularies directly. Lower is better.

## Variants

Nine runs, three learning rates for each model. All at 38M dense parameters (d = 512, 12 layers, SwiGLU 1024), 50M FineWeb-Edu base tokens, batch 64 × 512 positions, warmup 50, seed 1337. At the same batch in positions the macro models see about 56k base tokens per step against 32k, so they take 891 steps against 1,526.

| Model | AdamW 3e-3 | AdamW 1e-3 | AdamW 3e-4 |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| 8k/8k transformer (1,526 steps) | 1.4127 | **1.4087** (baseline) | 1.4395 |
| 64k/64k transformer on the macro tokenizer (891 steps) | **1.5602** | 1.5985 | 1.6944 |
| Fraise, 64k in, 8k out (891 steps) | **1.5408** | 1.5926 | 1.6795 |

## Reading the result

- One seed per run, so differences of a few thousandths (Fraise against the 64k/64k model at 1e-3, 0.006) may be noise.
- Both macro models are best at the top of the grid; a higher rate was never tried.
- The minibatch differs between runs: 16 for the two 3e-3 transformer runs (started before the runner switched to 64) and for all three Fraise runs (out of memory at 64), 64 for the others. A minibatch only splits the 64-sequence step into accumulated parts, so the results are comparable across it.
- All nine runs were imported from their files (commit d0fc54e, a separate worktree), not re-run under AblationKit. The gap audit later repeated two of them on newer code with the same seed: 1.4087 for the 8k/8k at 1e-3 and 1.5609 for the 64k/64k at 3e-3.
- The 8k/8k and 64k/64k runs kept untied embeddings at N(0,1) and had no final LayerNorm; with both fixed, the 64k/64k model's gap to the 8k/8k fell from 0.152 to 0.085 BPB. The macro models' preferred rate may differ once those faults are fixed; it has not been re-swept.

records.title: Base 8k vs symmetric 64k gap audit at 38M dense, 50M base tokens
records.summary: Compares the 8k/8k transformer with the 64k/64k transformer on the macro tokenizer at 38M parameters and 50M base tokens of text, adding two candidate fixes one at a time (embedding initialisation with standard deviation 0.02, then a final LayerNorm), to find out why the 64k model trailed by 0.152 bits per byte (BPB). With both fixes the gap fell to 0.085; halving the 64k model's batch to double its optimizer steps changed nothing (1.4996 against 1.4990); and a 64k/64k on a standard BPE with both fixes scored 1.4045, matching the 8k/8k transformer (1.4077 to 1.4139), so the rest of the gap belongs to the macro tokenizer. One seed per variant, at 38M parameters only.

variants.title: Base 8k, AdamW 1e-3, default N(0,1) embedding, no final norm
variants.description: The baseline: the 8k/8k transformer with the original settings (untied embeddings at PyTorch's N(0,1) initialisation, no final LayerNorm), AdamW 1e-3. It repeats the earlier sweep's best 8k/8k run on the current code.

variants.title: Symmetric 64k, AdamW 3e-3, default N(0,1) embedding, no final norm
variants.description: The 64k/64k transformer on the macro tokenizer with the original settings, AdamW 3e-3. Against the baseline it measures the gap before any fix (0.152 BPB).

variants.title: Base 8k, embedding init std 0.02
variants.description: The 8k/8k transformer with its input embedding table initialised with standard deviation 0.02 instead of N(0,1) (the output head is unchanged); no final LayerNorm. Tests the embedding-initialisation fix on the small vocabulary.

variants.title: Symmetric 64k, embedding init std 0.02
variants.description: The 64k/64k transformer on the macro tokenizer with embedding initialisation std 0.02; no final LayerNorm. Paired with base-emb002, it measures how much of the gap the embedding fix removes.

variants.title: Base 8k, embedding std 0.02 + final LayerNorm
variants.description: The 8k/8k transformer with both fixes: embedding std 0.02 and a LayerNorm between the last block and the output head.

variants.title: Symmetric 64k, embedding std 0.02 + final LayerNorm
variants.description: The 64k/64k transformer on the macro tokenizer with both fixes. Paired with base-emb002-finalnorm, it gives the gap that remains once both faults are fixed (0.085 BPB).

variants.title: Symmetric 64k, embedding std 0.02 + final LayerNorm, batch 32
variants.description: As sym-emb002-finalnorm, but with batch 32 instead of 64 sequences, so it takes 1,782 optimizer steps instead of 891 over the same text. Tests whether the 64k model trails because it takes fewer steps. Added after the study was created.

variants.title: 64k/64k on a standard BPE, embedding std 0.02 + final LayerNorm
variants.description: A 64k/64k transformer with both fixes on a standard word-pretokenized byte-level BPE (65,536 tokens, same trainer and pre-tokenizer as the 8k), instead of the cross-word macro tokenizer; budgets calibrated to the same text (1,186 steps). Separates the cost of a 64k vocabulary from the cost of the macro tokenizer. Added after the study was created.

records.protocol: Code: commit 72b1efb plus the uncommitted opt-in switches in data/ak/configs/gap/code.diff (final_norm, embedding_init_std; both off by default). Models: configs/base.json / symmetric.json (d=512, 12 layers, SwiGLU 1024, untied). Training: lr-sweep-38m protocol (configs sweep-{0.001,0.003}-mb16.json): 50M FineWeb-Edu base tokens, batch 64x512 positions, minibatch 16, Muon 0.02, warmup 50, wd 0.01, BF16 + compile, seed 1337, one seed. Validation once at the end on 262,144 held-out base tokens. Compare validation/bits_per_byte; the gap = sym - base for the same treatment. Exceptions: sym-emb002-finalnorm-b32 uses batch 32 (1,782 steps); bpe64k-emb002-finalnorm uses the standard 64k BPE tokenizer with budgets calibrated to the same text (38,849,560 training and 203,610 validation tokens of its own, 1,186 steps; validation covered 971,133 bytes against 971,115 for the 8k/8k). Jobs ran concurrently (up to four at a time), so throughput is not comparable across runs.
records.body:
## Why this comparison

In the 100M pilot and the 38M learning-rate sweep, the 64k/64k transformer on the macro tokenizer trailed the 8k/8k transformer by a wide margin (0.152 BPB at 38M, 0.064 at 100M). A code audit of both training paths found no bug in the loss, masking, packing, schedule or evaluation, but two non-standard choices that could weigh more on a 64k vocabulary: untied input embeddings left at PyTorch's N(0,1) initialisation, and no final LayerNorm before the output head. This study adds each fix to both models and measures how the gap moves, then runs two controls: more optimizer steps for the 64k model, and a 64k vocabulary built by a standard tokenizer.

Bits per byte (BPB) is the summed negative log-likelihood of the held-out targets, in bits, divided by the UTF-8 bytes those targets cover:

$$
\mathrm{BPB} = \frac{1}{B \ln 2} \sum_{t} -\ln p(x_t \mid x_{<t})
$$

where $B$ is the number of bytes scored. Unlike a per-token loss it does not depend on the tokenizer, so it compares models with 8k and 64k vocabularies directly. Lower is better.

The quantity tracked is the gap for the same treatment,

$$
\Delta = \mathrm{BPB}_{64\text{k}} - \mathrm{BPB}_{8\text{k}}
$$

## Variants

All runs: 38M dense parameters (d = 512, 12 layers, SwiGLU 1024, untied embeddings), 50M FineWeb-Edu base tokens of text, AdamW 1e-3 for the 8k/8k and 3e-3 for the 64k models (the best rates of the earlier sweep), Muon 0.02, seed 1337.

| Variant | Model | Embedding init | Final LayerNorm | Batch (steps) | BPB |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | ---: |
| base-default (baseline) | 8k/8k transformer | N(0,1) | no | 64 (1,526) | 1.4087 |
| sym-default | 64k/64k, macro tokenizer | N(0,1) | no | 64 (891) | 1.5609 |
| base-emb002 | 8k/8k transformer | std 0.02 | no | 64 (1,526) | 1.4077 |
| sym-emb002 | 64k/64k, macro tokenizer | std 0.02 | no | 64 (891) | 1.5180 |
| base-emb002-finalnorm | 8k/8k transformer | std 0.02 | yes | 64 (1,526) | 1.4139 |
| sym-emb002-finalnorm | 64k/64k, macro tokenizer | std 0.02 | yes | 64 (891) | 1.4990 |
| sym-emb002-finalnorm-b32 | 64k/64k, macro tokenizer | std 0.02 | yes | 32 (1,782) | 1.4996 |
| bpe64k-emb002-finalnorm | 64k/64k, standard BPE | std 0.02 | yes | 64 (1,186) | 1.4045 |

The gap for each treatment: 0.152 with neither fix, 0.110 with the embedding fix, 0.085 with both, 0.086 with both at batch 32, and −0.009 for the standard 64k BPE with both.

A "final LayerNorm only" variant was planned but never run and has been removed from the list, so the final norm's effect without the embedding fix is not measured.

## Reading the result

- One seed per variant. Differences under about 0.01 BPB, such as the 8k/8k with and without the final norm (+0.006) or the standard 64k BPE against the 8k/8k (−0.009), are not resolved.
- The two original-settings runs repeat two imported sweep runs with the same seed and configuration on a later commit (with the new switches off): 1.4087 against 1.4087 for the 8k/8k and 1.5609 against 1.5602 for the 64k/64k. That shows the opt-in code changes did not alter default training; it is not an estimate of seed noise.
- The standard 64k BPE was trained on the same FineWeb-Edu slice as the macro tokenizer, while the 8k tokenizer was trained on a broader mix (BabyLM, Cosmopedia and FineWeb-Edu), so the 64k BPE is more in-domain. Its budgets count its own tokens and were calibrated to cover the same text.
- Jobs ran up to four at a time on the same machine, so `tokens_per_second` is not comparable across runs.
- The full reading, with the attribution of the gap, is in the gap audit's final report.
